one_liner: Scala/Java gRPC on Pekko HTTP and Pekko Streams; out-served the stock C++ async gRPC greeter 1.27-1.73x in one grpc_bench run.
what_it_does: Apache Pekko gRPC generates Scala or Java service traits, clients and a Pekko HTTP request handler from .proto files through sbt, Maven or Gradle plugins; you implement methods that return Futures (unary) or Pekko Streams Sources (streaming) and bind the generated HttpRequest => Future[HttpResponse] handler with Pekko HTTP's HTTP/2 server. Clients are built on grpc-java's shaded Netty transport. It speaks standard gRPC over HTTP/2, so any gRPC client can call it, but the server code is a rewrite on the Pekko programming model, not a drop-in for a C++ gRPC server.
how_it_is_fast: The benchmark gives no mechanism. What the server does: requests are served by Pekko HTTP's own HTTP/2 implementation on Pekko Streams (not by gRPC C++ core or grpc-java's Netty server), entities are collected strictly and dispatched to a Future-returning handler on a fork-join dispatcher capped at the container's CPU count, all JIT-compiled on the HotSpot JVM. In the April 2026 run the C++ server burned more CPU per request (405.58% CPU for 85485 req/s at 4 CPUs against 270.92% for 142375 req/s), which points at the C++ side's library build and server pattern rather than any trick in Pekko.
when_to_use: You already run Pekko (or are migrating from Akka gRPC) and want gRPC endpoints that share the actor system, dispatcher and Pekko Streams backpressure for streaming RPCs.

Unary or streaming gRPC services on 2-4 cores where throughput per container matters more than memory: in grpc_bench #559 it reached 120-142k req/s at 2-4 CPUs on a Xeon Gold 6548N, ahead of the stock C++ greeter and rust_tonic_mt.
JVM shops that want one generated API for Scala and Java with sbt, Maven or Gradle builds.
Services where p50/average latency under heavy concurrency matters (5.23 ms average against 11.28 ms for the C++ greeter at 4 CPUs in #559).
when_not_to_use: Memory-constrained deployments: the Pekko server averaged 450-998 MiB in #559 against 21-32 MiB for the C++ server (largely JVM heap sizing, but a JVM floor of hundreds of MiB remains).
Tail-latency-critical paths: p99 at 4 CPUs was 22.14 ms against 19.69 ms for C++, and JIT warm-up plus GC pauses affect short-lived or bursty processes.
Single-core containers: in other grpc_bench runs (#441 on an i9-13900KF) it trailed cpp_grpc_mt at 1 and 2 CPUs (0.89x and 0.97x), and one 1-CPU result in #475 collapsed to 5661 req/s.
If raw JVM gRPC throughput is the goal and you are not tied to Pekko: Vert.x gRPC posted more req/s than Pekko at 1 and 2 CPUs in the same #559 run.
Teams that need a stable 2.x API now: the repo tracks Pekko 2.0 and pekko-http 2.0 milestones, and the README warns APIs and build plugins may still change.

integration.dependencies: Pekko actor and streams, Pekko HTTP (server side, HTTP/2 enabled), grpc-java grpc-netty-shaded (client side), generated protobuf classes via the sbt/Maven/Gradle plugin
integration.min_toolchain: JDK 17+ (README); Scala 2.13 default, other cross-built Scala versions not listed in the README; the benchmark used Scala 2.13.17 on Temurin 23
integration.thread_safety: not documented in the pages read; service methods return Futures and run on the Pekko default dispatcher, so implementations must be safe for concurrent calls.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — wire-compatible gRPC over HTTP/2, so existing clients keep working, but the C++ server must be rewritten in Scala or Java against the generated Pekko traits.

gotchas: Harness flaw on the C++ side: grpc_bench's cpp_grpc_mt keeps exactly one pre-posted RequestSayHello per completion queue and does a new/delete of CallData per RPC, whereas gRPC's own async QPS benchmark server (test/cpp/qps/server_async.cc) pre-posts 5000 request contexts per queue, so the baseline is the tutorial pattern, not gRPC C++ at its fastest.

The C++ server links Debian-packaged libgrpc++ installed by unpinned apt-get on the gcc:15.2.0 image; that image line is built on Debian trixie (docker-library gcc 15 Dockerfile FROM buildpack-deps:trixie), whose grpc package is 1.51.1 per Debian package listings seen in search snippets, many releases behind upstream gRPC (pekko-grpc itself moved to grpc-java 1.84.2 on 2026-10-10). The exact version was not recorded by the run, so this is an inference.

Memory figures in grpc_bench come from docker stats with -XX:MinRAMPercentage=70 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 on a 4096m container, so the JVM row reflects a pre-sized heap more than its working set; tune heap flags before judging memory.

The published win was measured with Pekko 1.2.1, pekko-http 1.3.0 and ParallelGC at grpc_bench c4c93b3; the benchmark now builds Pekko 2.0 milestones with SerialGC, and no run of that configuration is published; the 1.27-1.73x margin comes from one 120 s run per CPU count, while other runs show 0.89-1.15x.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Armeria, Vert.x gRPC or grpc-dotnet when the service already lives in a Pekko actor system or uses Pekko Streams for streaming RPCs; for raw unary throughput on few cores Vert.x gRPC posted higher numbers in the same #559 run, and tonic gives similar req/s at a fraction of the memory.
verified_claims_summary: In grpc_bench discussion #559 (maintainer run, commit c4c93b3, Xeon Gold 6548N, server capped at 1-4 CPUs via docker --cpus, ghz 50 connections and 1000 concurrent unary echo calls, 120 s after 30 s warm-up), scala_pekko on Pekko 1.2.1 and Temurin 23 served 72808-142375 req/s against 57403-85485 req/s for the C++ async greeter built with g++ 15.2.0 -O3 -flto on Debian-packaged libgrpc++ (1.27x at 1 CPU up to 1.73x at 3 CPUs). Earlier published runs put the two within 0.89-1.15x of each other, so the size of the gap depends on the run and on a C++ baseline that is neither pinned nor tuned.
status_note: Actively maintained Apache project (commits through 2026-10-10, currently tracking Pekko and pekko-http 2.0 milestones) under Apache-2.0 and usable as a library today, but the catalogue's speed claim rests on one benchmark run against an untuned tutorial-pattern C++ server built on an unpinned distro gRPC.
